title: Chroma Town
subject: How colour works
bigIdea: Colour is three numbers: three lights on a screen, three signals in the eye.
learner: A curious adult with no background in colour science who uses screens and printers every day.
goals: Predict the result of mixing coloured lights.

goals.text: Predict the result of mixing inks, the mirror image of mixing lights.

goals: Describe a colour with hue, saturation and lightness and relate it to RGB.
Explain why three numbers are enough to describe a colour, and why the same numbers can look different.

sources.title: Standard colour science as found in any introductory text (additive and subtractive mixing, HSL, simultaneous contrast, trichromacy)
sources.note: No user material: this example course was written from general reference knowledge. The cone curves in the lab are simplified.

sources.title: Malacara, Color Vision and Colorimetry: Theory and Applications (SPIE Press), chapter 1
sources.note: Newton’s prism experiments and his 1672 communication to the Royal Society; Young 1802; Helmholtz.

sources.title: Yellott, Important Dates in Vision Science
sources.note: Young’s three-receptor theory; Hering’s opponent theory in the 1870s; CIE 1931.

sources.title: The Victorian Web, Nineteenth-Century Photography: A Timeline

The works themselves: Hering, Zur Lehre vom Lichtsinne (1878); Munsell, A Color Notation (1905); CIE 1931 standard observer; Stokes et al., A Standard Default Color Space for the Internet: sRGB (1996)
sources.note: Publication dates taken from the works; not re-read for this example.

sources.title: W3C, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, definition of relative luminance
sources.note: The sRGB formula from a value 0 to 255 to linear light (threshold 0.04045, exponent 2.4) and the weights 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B. Used upstairs in Three Lamps House and in the Painter's safe.

themes.name: Lamp Quarter
themes.idea: Light adds up. Ink takes away.

themes.name: Sight Hill
themes.idea: Colour happens in the eye and the brain, not in the object.

cue.why: A hill is where you go to look: this theme is about the observer.

themes.name: Old Town
themes.idea: Three centuries to find out why three numbers are enough.

cue.why: Old trees and standing stones for the origins of the ideas.

concepts.name: Additive mixing
concepts.objective: Predict the colour of any mix of red, green and blue light.
concepts.idea: A screen makes every colour by adding red, green and blue light. All three together make white.
concepts.wrongBelief: Mixing colours always works like paint: more colours give a darker, muddier result.

anchor.text: Three torches with coloured gels pointed at the same wall.
anchor.limits: Real torches are not pure red, green and blue, so their white is less clean than a screen’s.

concepts.application: Every screen works this way, and the colour picker of any app shows these three numbers.
remember: Red + green light = yellow. All three lights = white.
A pixel is three numbers: red, green, blue, each from 0 to 255.

explain.q: Why does adding a second lamp never make the wall darker?
explain.a: A lamp only adds light to what the wall already sends back. Nothing in the process removes light, so the sum can only grow.

stations.goal: Lights add up: where two lamps overlap, the wall gets both colours at once.
stations.object: Three coloured lamps on a dark wall.
stations.action: Drags the lamps until their light overlaps, and points at the wall to read which lights are on.
stations.surprise: Red over green turns yellow, and all three turn white: brighter, not muddy.

predict.q: Red light on top of green light will look...
predict.why: Red light and green light add up, and the eye sees their sum as yellow.

tries: Drag the red lamp onto the green one.
Bring all three lamps together.
stations.takeaway: Red and green light make yellow, green and blue make cyan, red and blue make magenta, and all three together make white. Adding light can only make the wall brighter, because nothing in the mix takes light away.
stations.source: Drawn live with additive blending: each lamp adds its own channel.

stations.goal: A pixel is three tiny lamps. Its colour is three numbers from 0 to 255.
stations.object: One pixel, magnified into its three stripes.
stations.action: Sets the three brightness values, then steps back from the screen.
stations.surprise: The stripes can no longer be told apart and a single colour appears, though only red, green and blue are drawn.
controls: Brightness of the red, green and blue lamp (one group of three sliders)
tries: Make orange: a lot of red, some green, no blue.
Make a mid grey: three equal numbers.
Step back until the stripes merge into one colour.
stations.takeaway: Every colour on a screen is three numbers, (red, green, blue), and equal numbers give a grey. The eye cannot resolve the three small lamps of a pixel, so it sees their sum.
stations.source: On the left only pure red, green and blue stripes are drawn. Any other colour you see there is made by your eye.

stations.goal: Screen numbers are not amounts of light: 128 sends out far less than half of what 255 does.
stations.object: A patch of fine black and white lines beside a flat grey patch.
stations.action: Sets the grey value until the flat patch matches the lines, reading how much light it sends out.
stations.surprise: 128 is much darker than the lines: the match is near 188.

predict.q: Fine lines, half black and half white, send out half the light of white. Which grey matches them?
predict.why: Screen values sit on a curve: 188 sends out about half the light of 255, and 128 only about a fifth.

tries: Set the grey to 128 and compare it with the lines.
Find the grey that sends out half the light: watch the read-out.
stations.takeaway: Screen numbers are not amounts of light, because sRGB places them on a curve: 128 sends out about 22% of the light of white, and half the light is reached near 188.
stations.source: Light computed live with the sRGB formula in the WCAG 2.1 definition of relative luminance. The lines match the flat grey only on a screen close to sRGB, seen at 100% zoom: yours may be a few steps off.

page.title: Lights add
page.text: When a red lamp shines on a dark wall, the wall sends red light to the eye. A green lamp on the same spot adds green light, so the wall now sends red and green together. Nothing in this process takes light away, which is why two lamps are always brighter than one.

figure.caption: Three lamps drifting together. Where all three overlap the wall is white.

page.title: A pixel is three lamps
page.text: Under a magnifying glass every pixel of a screen splits into a red, a green and a blue stripe, and each stripe has a brightness from 0 to 255. From a normal distance the eye cannot separate the stripes, so it sees their sum as a single colour.

questions.q: Red light plus green light gives...
questions.why: Lights add. Red and green together stimulate the eye like yellow does.
traps: Mixing paints gives a muddy brown, so it feels natural for lights too; but lights add up, and red plus green light makes the eye see yellow.
Purple is what red and blue make together; green is the other light here, and red plus green gives yellow.
White needs all three lights; with only red and green, blue is missing, and the sum is yellow.

questions.q: Red, green and blue light at full strength give...
questions.why: Adding light always makes the result brighter. All three at full strength is white.
traps: In paint, more colours make a darker mix; light works the other way: every lamp you add makes the wall brighter.
Equal amounts do give a grey, but at full strength the grey is as light as it can be: white.
Brown is what paints do when mixed; three lights at full strength add up to the brightest colour, white.

questions.q: On a screen, the colour of a pixel is stored as...
options: Three numbers: red, green and blue
questions.why: Each pixel has a red, a green and a blue lamp, each with its own brightness from 0 to 255.
traps: One number would be enough for brightness alone; a colour needs a value for each of the three lamps of the pixel.
Light can be described by its wavelength, but a screen has no lamp for each colour: it mixes three.

questions.q: A pixel is set to R 120, G 120, B 120. What do you see?
questions.why: Equal amounts of the three lights have no hue. The amount sets how light the grey is.
traps: Red is the first number, so it is easy to read it alone; but all three are equal, and equal amounts have no hue.
Equal lights might seem to cancel each other; lights only add, so three equal lights make a grey, not darkness.
Three equal lights do give a neutral colour, but 120 is about half of 255: the result is a mid grey, not white.

questions.q: A pixel shows yellow. Which sub-pixel is switched off?
questions.why: Yellow on a screen is red plus green. Blue stays dark.
traps: Green is one of the two lights that make yellow; switch it off and only red is left.
Red is one of the two lights that make yellow; switch it off and only green is left.
A yellow lamp would be the simplest explanation, but a pixel has only red, green and blue: yellow is red plus green.

questions.q: A web designer wants a pixel to show magenta. Which of its lamps are on?
questions.why: Red light plus blue light gives magenta. Green stays dark.
traps: Red and green together give yellow, not magenta; magenta needs blue instead of green.
Green and blue together give cyan; magenta needs red with the blue.
A magenta lamp would be the simple answer, but a pixel has only red, green and blue: magenta is red plus blue.

further.title: WCAG 2.1: relative luminance
further.why: The exact formula from the three numbers of a pixel to the light it sends out.

riddles.clue: pw = red lamp + blue lamp. One word. Don't forget it AGAIN.

inside.note: Notes for the next experiment. A screen's yellow is red light plus green light, with no yellow light in it at all, and a pure yellow light can look exactly the same because the eye keeps only three signals (see the Cone Cave). The next thing to test is whether 128, half of 255, also sends out half of the light.

concepts.name: Subtractive mixing
concepts.objective: Explain why printers use cyan, magenta and yellow, and why mixing inks gets darker.
concepts.idea: Ink works by removing light from white paper. Each ink removes one of the three lights.
concepts.wrongBelief: Ink adds its colour to the paper, the way a lamp adds light.

anchor.text: The same two colours mixed as lights and as inks, side by side.
anchor.limits: Real inks are not perfect filters: three of them give a muddy dark, which is why printers add black.

concepts.application: The cartridges of a printer: cyan, magenta and yellow, plus black for a deeper dark.
remember: Cyan absorbs red, magenta absorbs green, yellow absorbs blue.
More ink, less light: mixed inks get darker.
On paper, tone is the size of the dots.

explain.q: Why do printers use cyan, magenta and yellow, and not red, green and blue inks?
explain.a: Cyan, magenta and yellow each remove one of the three lights, so they can be layered and still leave something. A red, green or blue ink removes two at once: any two of them on top of each other leave nothing.

callbacks.how: The same three lights as in Three Lamps House, now taken away instead of added.

stations.goal: Paper is white because it sends back all light. An ink works by keeping some of it.
stations.object: Three transparent ink discs on white paper.
stations.action: Drags the inks over each other and points at the paper to read which light comes back.
stations.surprise: Stacking all three leaves black: the opposite of the three lamps.
tries: Drag cyan onto yellow and read what comes back.
Stack all three inks.
stations.takeaway: Cyan absorbs red, magenta absorbs green and yellow absorbs blue. Two inks together leave one of the three lights, and all three leave none, which the eye sees as black.
stations.source: Drawn live with multiply blending: each ink removes its own channel.

predict.q: Cyan ink printed over yellow ink on white paper will look...
predict.why: Cyan absorbs the red light and yellow absorbs the blue: only green comes back.

stations.goal: The same colours behave in opposite ways as lights and as paints.
stations.object: The same three colour names, as lamps on a dark wall and as paints on white paper, side by side.
stations.action: Switches each colour on and off and compares the two sides.
stations.surprise: With nothing on, the lamp side is black and the paper side white. With everything on they swap.
controls: Three on/off switches: red, green, blue
tries: Switch on all three.
Compare none with two.
stations.takeaway: Lights start from dark and add, so more lights give a brighter colour. Paints start from white paper and take light away, so more paints give a darker one.
stations.source: Idealised lights and paints: each paint is taken to reflect one primary only.

stations.goal: A printer cannot make light grey ink. It prints black dots of different sizes.
stations.object: A printed photograph of a shaded ball.
stations.surprise: The smooth greys are black dots of different sizes on white paper.
tries: Step closer until you see single dots.
Compare the print with the original tones.
stations.takeaway: Tone on paper comes from the size of the dots, with big dots looking dark and small dots looking light, because from reading distance the eye averages ink and paper.
stations.source: A halftone computed live from a simple shaded ball.

page.title: Ink takes away
page.text: Paper has no lamps of its own and looks white because it reflects all the light that falls on it. An ink works as a filter on that light. Cyan ink, for example, absorbs red light and lets green and blue come back, so the paper looks cyan where it is printed.

figure.caption: Three inks drifting together. Where all three overlap, no light comes back.

page.title: Three inks instead of red, green and blue
page.text: A red ink absorbs green and blue, which is two thirds of the light at once, so a green ink printed on top of it leaves nothing to come back. Cyan, magenta and yellow each remove only one third of the light, and this is why they can be layered and combined.

page.title: Tone from dots
page.text: A printer either puts ink on a spot or does not. Light and dark come from the size of the dots, which the eye averages from reading distance.

questions.q: Cyan ink looks cyan because it absorbs...
questions.why: White minus red leaves green plus blue, which is cyan.
traps: Cyan does look a bit bluish, so it seems to keep blue; in fact it sends blue back and removes red.
Cyan looks greenish-blue, which is the hint: it sends green back, so green is not what it removes.
Black ink absorbs everything; a coloured ink removes only one of the three lights, or the paper would look black.

questions.q: Mixing more inks makes the result...
questions.why: Every ink removes some light. More inks, less light left.
traps: That is the rule of lights, where adding makes brighter; ink starts from white paper and takes light away.
More ink can look like more colour, but each ink removes light, so the mix gets darker and duller.
White is what three lights make together; three inks together remove almost all the light and give near black.

questions.q: How does a printer make a light grey with black ink?
questions.why: It prints ink or no ink. Small dots leave more white paper, and the eye averages the two.
traps: Watering ink down is how a painter makes it lighter; a printer cannot dilute its ink: it prints ink or no ink.
A thinner layer sounds plausible, but a printer cannot vary the thickness of its ink; it changes the size of its dots.

questions.q: Yellow ink over magenta ink on white paper gives...
questions.why: Yellow removes blue, magenta removes green. Only red is left.
traps: Blue is a light that yellow ink removes, so it cannot come back from yellow ink.
Green is the light that magenta ink removes, so it cannot come back from magenta ink.
Two inks remove two lights, not all three; the third light, red, still comes back from the paper.

questions.q: A printed photo has smooth greys. Up close you would see...
questions.why: A printer puts ink or no ink. Tone comes from the size of the dots; the eye averages them.
traps: A smooth grey suggests grey ink, but a printer cannot dilute its ink: tone comes from the size of black dots.
Several grey inks would also make smooth greys, but tone in print comes from black dots of different sizes on white paper.
Tiny lamps are how a screen makes colour; paper sends no light of its own, it only reflects it.

concepts.name: Hue, saturation, lightness

expert.name: Marta
expert.line: I never mix by numbers. I ask three things: which colour, how far from grey, how close to white or black.

concepts.objective: Describe any colour with three words (which colour, how vivid, how light) and link them to RGB.
concepts.idea: Hue, saturation and lightness are the same colours as RGB, described the way people talk.
concepts.wrongBelief: RGB and hue, saturation, lightness are different sets of colours.

anchor.text: RGB is a street address; hue, saturation and lightness are directions given by a neighbour.
anchor.limits: The conversion is exact, but equal steps on a dial do not look equal to the eye.

concepts.application: Design tools and CSS accept a colour as hsl(), because changing one dial is easier than changing three numbers together.
remember: Hue = which colour (the angle on the wheel).
Lightness = how close to white or black.

explain.q: A designer says "same colour, just less loud". Which dial moves, and what happens to the three RGB numbers?
explain.a: Saturation goes down. The three RGB numbers move toward each other; when they are equal the colour has become a grey.

callbacks.how: Every position on the wheel is shown also as the three lamp numbers of Three Lamps House.

stations.goal: Any colour can be described the way people talk: which colour, how vivid, how light.
stations.object: A colour disc where the angle is hue and the distance from the centre is saturation.
stations.action: Drags a marker on the disc and changes lightness to reach a named colour.
stations.surprise: At the centre every hue becomes the same grey, and the three RGB numbers become equal.
tries: Find a pastel pink: a red hue, vivid, and very light.
Turn any colour into a grey without touching lightness.
stations.takeaway: Hue is which colour, saturation how far it is from grey, lightness how close to white or black. It is the same colour as RGB, with the numbers rearranged.
stations.source: HSL computed live from the standard conversion to RGB.

page.title: Three dials
page.text: People rarely describe a colour with its three screen numbers: they ask for something more orange, less vivid or lighter. Hue, saturation and lightness turn those three words into three dials, so that a colour can be adjusted the way people talk about it.

page.title: The same colours
page.text: HSL does not add any colour to RGB. It is a different set of coordinates for the same points, the way a town can be described by street addresses or by walking directions.

questions.q: Which dial turns red into orange into yellow?
questions.why: Hue is the position around the colour wheel.
traps: Saturation changes how vivid a colour is, not which colour it is; red stays red, only duller or more vivid.
Lightness changes how close to white or black a colour is, not which colour it is.
Contrast is a real word for differences between colours, but it is not one of the three dials.

questions.q: Saturation at zero gives...
questions.why: With no saturation there is no hue left: only a grey whose lightness you chose.
traps: Black is what lightness at zero gives; saturation at zero keeps the lightness and removes the hue.
White is what lightness at the top gives; saturation at zero keeps the lightness and removes the hue.
Full saturation is the pure colour; zero is the other end of the scale, where no colour is left.

questions.q: Which dial turns a red into a dark red and then into black?
questions.why: Lowering lightness moves any colour toward black without changing which colour it is.
traps: A dark red can look like a different colour, maroon or brown; but the hue stays red, only the lightness goes down.
A darker red also looks duller, which points to saturation; but saturation heads toward grey, not toward black.

questions.q: Pastel pink is a red with...
questions.why: Same hue as red, pushed toward white.
traps: Pastel colours are soft, which can sound like low; but low lightness heads toward black, and pink is red toward white.
Pink has its own name, so it seems to be its own hue; on the wheel it sits where red is, only lighter.
Pink is softer than red, which suggests less saturation; but zero saturation would leave a grey, not pink.

questions.q: You keep a colour's hue and saturation and slide its lightness to 100%. What do you get?
questions.why: Lightness is how close to white or black: at the top every colour becomes white.
traps: The pure colour sits at lightness 50%; going higher moves it toward white.
Black is the other end of the lightness dial, at 0%.
A grey comes from saturation at zero; lightness at the top gives white whatever the saturation.

questions.q: In HSL a colour has saturation 0 and lightness 50%. What are its red, green and blue numbers?
options: Only red is set; green and blue are 0
questions.why: No saturation means no hue: a grey, and on a screen a grey is three equal numbers. Lightness 50% puts them about halfway up.
traps: 255, 0, 0 is pure red at full saturation; with saturation at zero no hue is left.
0, 0, 0 is black, which needs lightness 0%; at 50% the grey is in the middle.
Hue 0 is red on the wheel, but with saturation at zero the hue no longer counts: all three numbers are equal.

riddles.clue: Combination: where my green sits on the wheel. In degrees. M.

inside.note: Marta's note. Lightness on my dials is not how light a colour looks. At lightness 50%, pure yellow sends out about thirteen times as much light as pure blue, because the eye weighs green most and blue least (0.2126 red + 0.7152 green + 0.0722 blue, in linear light). That is why my yellows never sit quietly next to my blues.

concepts.name: Colour depends on context

expert.name: Bruno
expert.line: A skein that matched in the vat can look wrong on the shelf. I judge every colour against what will sit next to it.

concepts.objective: Show that the same patch looks different on different backgrounds, and say why that matters.
concepts.idea: The eye judges a colour against what surrounds it. The same numbers can look different.
concepts.wrongBelief: The eye measures colour like an instrument: same numbers, same appearance.

anchor.text: A grey card looks light in a dark room and dark on fresh snow.
anchor.limits: The surround changes how a colour looks, not what a camera or a file records.

concepts.application: Checking the colour of text or of a chart on its real background before publishing.
remember: The same numbers can look different on different backgrounds.
A dark surround makes a patch look lighter; a coloured surround pushes it toward the opposite colour.

explain.q: Why is it a bad idea to compare two colour swatches that sit on different backgrounds?
explain.a: The eye judges each swatch against its own surround, so the comparison measures the backgrounds as much as the swatches. Put both on the same neutral background.

callbacks.how: Lightness was a dial in the Painter's House. Here the same lightness looks different.

stations.goal: The eye does not measure a colour. It compares it with what is around it.
stations.object: Two grey squares on a wall that goes from dark to light.
stations.action: Drags one square next to the other, then swaps the wall for a plain one.
stations.surprise: Side by side they are the same grey.

predict.q: Two grey squares, one on the dark side and one on the light side. Which is lighter?
options: The one on the dark side
The one on the light side
predict.why: Both squares are the same grey, 128, 128, 128. The surround changes how they look.

tries: Drag one square next to the other.
Replace the wall with a plain one.
stations.takeaway: The two squares have the same numbers. On a dark surround a patch looks lighter and on a light surround it looks darker, an effect called simultaneous contrast.
stations.source: Drawn live: the wall is a gradient, the squares are flat fills computed by the same code.

stations.goal: The surround shifts hue as well, not only lightness.
stations.object: Two neutral patches, one on a yellow wall and one on a blue wall.
stations.action: Covers the coloured walls and brings them back.
stations.surprise: The tint of the patches goes away with the walls.

predict.q: The small patch on the yellow wall and the one on the blue wall: are they the same colour?
options: No, the one on yellow is bluer
No, the one on blue is bluer
predict.why: Both patches are the same neutral grey. The wall around each one tints how it looks.

tries: Cover the coloured walls.
Bring the walls back and look again.
stations.takeaway: A neutral patch takes on the opposite of its surround, so it looks bluish on a yellow wall and yellowish on a blue one. For this reason a colour is best judged on the background it will be used on.
stations.source: Drawn live: the walls and the patches are flat fills.

page.title: The eye compares
page.text: The eye evolved to recognise surfaces under changing light rather than to measure light, and for this it judges every patch against its neighbours. A grey patch on black therefore looks light, while the same patch on white looks dark.

page.title: Why it matters
page.text: Since the eye compares, a colour should be chosen on the background where it will be used. Two charts with different backgrounds can make the same value look different, and equal numbers in a file do not promise an equal appearance.

questions.q: Two patches have identical RGB values. Can they look different?
questions.why: Perceived colour depends on the surround. The numbers stay the same.
traps: If the eye measured colour like an instrument, the same numbers would always look the same; it compares with the surround instead.
Old screens can show colours badly, but this happens on any screen and on paper: the cause is the eye.
Print has its own quirks, but this happens on screens too: the eye judges a colour against its neighbours.

questions.q: A neutral grey patch on a yellow wall looks slightly...
questions.why: The eye pushes a neutral patch away from its surround, toward the opposite colour.
traps: It is easy to expect the yellow to rub off on the patch; the eye does the opposite and pushes it away from yellow, toward blue.
If the eye were a measuring instrument the grey would stay neutral; it compares with the wall and shifts the patch.

questions.q: A grey patch on a dark background looks...
questions.why: The eye exaggerates the difference from the surround: simultaneous contrast.
traps: It seems natural that a dark surround would darken the patch; the eye exaggerates the difference, so the patch looks lighter.
If the eye measured light, nothing would change; it compares the patch with the background and shifts it.
Bluish is what a yellow surround does to a grey; a dark surround changes how light the patch looks, not its hue.

questions.q: You pick a text colour by eye on a dark mock-up. On a white page it looks wrong. Why?
questions.why: Judge a colour on the background it will actually be used on.
traps: When a colour looks wrong, it is tempting to blame the file; the numbers did not change, the background did.
White pages are brighter, but that alone does not change the text's numbers; what changes is the comparison the eye makes.
RGB numbers are exact; the same numbers look different because the eye judges them against a new surround.

questions.q: Two identical grey squares sit side by side, one on a black wall and one on a white wall. Which looks darker?
options: The one on the white wall
The one on the black wall
Neither: they are the same grey
questions.why: The eye exaggerates the difference from the surround: on white the grey looks darker, on black it looks lighter.
traps: It feels as if a dark wall should darken what sits on it; the eye does the opposite and makes that square look lighter.
The numbers are the same, but the eye judges each square against its own wall, so they do not look the same.

questions.q: A photographer judges a grey card lying on a bright red tablecloth and finds it slightly blue-green. What should she do before trusting her eye?
options: Add a little red to the card in the photo
Look at it again under a brighter lamp
Measure the card, or look at it against a neutral grey
questions.why: A coloured surround pushes a neutral patch toward the opposite colour, so the red cloth makes the grey look blue-green. A measurement or a neutral background removes the trick.
traps: Adding red would fix a card that really is blue-green, but the tint is in the eye, caused by the red cloth.
The eye is not a measuring instrument: it shifts the grey away from the red around it.
More light makes everything brighter, but the red cloth is still there and the eye still compares the card with it.

riddles.clue: Password? Bruno's name for the trick the dark wall played on the grey square. Two words.

inside.note: From Bruno's notebook. The same comparison that fooled you with the grey squares keeps a white shirt looking white under orange lamplight and under blue daylight, because the eye judges a surface against its neighbours rather than by the light itself. A camera cannot do this on its own, which is why it needs a white balance.

concepts.name: How we found out
concepts.objective: Place the key discoveries about colour in order and say what each one settled.
concepts.idea: From Newton’s prism to sRGB: each step turned colour from a mystery into numbers.
concepts.wrongBelief: Describing colour with three numbers is a convention of computers.
concepts.application: sRGB is why the same photo looks roughly alike on a phone and on a laptop.
remember: 1672, Newton: white light is a mixture.
1802, Young: three kinds of receptor are enough.
1931, CIE: colour as three measured numbers.

callbacks.how: Maxwell’s photograph of 1861 is Three Lamps House with three projectors.

timeline.title: White light is a mixture
timeline.text: Newton passes sunlight through a prism and gets a band of colours, and a second prism brings them back to white. This shows that the colour is already in the light and is not added by the glass.
timeline.why: The start of everything in the Lamp Quarter: lights can be split and added.
timeline.src: Newton, letter to the Royal Society, 1672

timeline.title: Three kinds of receptor
timeline.text: Young argues that the eye cannot hold a separate receptor for every colour. Three kinds, each answering to a broad range of light, would be enough.
timeline.why: This is the reason why three lamps are enough on a screen.

timeline.title: The first colour photograph
timeline.text: Three black-and-white photographs of a tartan ribbon, taken through red, green and blue filters and projected through the same filters, combine into a colour image.
timeline.why: It puts Young's idea to work, since three channels are enough to rebuild a coloured scene.

timeline.title: Opponent colours
timeline.text: In the 1870s Hering notes that nobody sees a reddish green or a yellowish blue. He proposes that vision works in opposing pairs: red against green, blue against yellow, light against dark.
timeline.why: Both views turned out to be right, with the three receptors first and the opposing pairs formed after them.

timeline.title: Colour gets coordinates
timeline.text: A painter and teacher, Munsell orders colours by hue, value and chroma, with steps that look equal to the eye.
timeline.why: The ancestor of the three dials in the Painter's House.

timeline.title: The standard observer
timeline.text: The International Commission on Illumination publishes colour-matching functions measured on human observers. Any light can now be written as three numbers that predict whether two lights will match.
timeline.why: Colour becomes measurable and comparable between laboratories.

timeline.title: sRGB
timeline.text: A shared default for what the three numbers of a pixel mean on an ordinary monitor. It becomes the standard colour space of the web.
timeline.why: Why the same file looks roughly the same on different screens.

questions.q: Who showed that white light is a mixture of colours?
questions.why: Newton, with two prisms, in 1672.
traps: Young is famous for colour, but his idea was three kinds of receptor in the eye, not the prism.
Maxwell worked with colour too, but he made the three-colour photograph, almost two centuries after the prism.
Munsell gave colours a notation in 1905; the prism experiment is much older, from 1672.

questions.q: Who argued in 1802 that three kinds of receptor are enough?
questions.why: Young reasoned that the eye could not hold a separate receptor for every colour.
traps: Newton is the best-known name in colour, but his discovery was that white light is a mixture, with prisms.
Munsell is known for a way of naming colours, from 1905; the three receptors were Young's idea, a century earlier.

questions.q: What did the CIE publish in 1931?
options: The standard observer: three measured numbers
questions.why: Colour-matching functions measured on people: any light becomes three numbers that predict a match.
traps: A colour photograph sounds like a natural milestone, but that was Maxwell in 1861, seventy years before.
sRGB is a standard for screens too, but it came in 1996, long after 1931.

questions.q: Maxwell’s 1861 photograph used...
questions.why: Red, green and blue filters: three channels, as a screen does today.
traps: A single colour plate would be the simple way, but colour plates did not exist yet: he used three filtered pictures.
Colour photographs were often painted by hand in that century, but Maxwell's colour came from three filters.
A prism splits light, as in Newton's experiment; Maxwell used red, green and blue filters instead.

further.title: Important Dates in Vision Science (J. Yellott)
further.why: A year-by-year list of discoveries about vision, from 1600 to 1960.

further.title: Nineteenth-Century Photography: A Timeline (The Victorian Web)
further.why: Where Maxwell's three-colour photograph sits in the story of photography.

concepts.name: Why three numbers are enough
concepts.objective: Explain how two physically different lights can look identical.
concepts.idea: The eye reduces any light to three signals. Lights that give the same three signals look the same.
concepts.wrongBelief: To show a colour, a device must emit light of that colour.

anchor.text: Three judges each give one score, and two very different performances can get the same three scores.
anchor.limits: Judges score independently. The three cone curves overlap, and that overlap is exactly why a mixture can imitate a pure light.

concepts.application: A display with three lamps per pixel reproduces most of the colours we can see.
remember: The eye keeps three signals for any light.
Different lights that give the same three signals look identical: metamers.

explain.q: A screen has no yellow lamp. Explain to a friend how it shows a lemon.
explain.a: It lights the red and the green lamp together. That excites the long and medium cones in the same proportion as the yellow light of a lemon would, so the brain receives the same signals and sees the same colour.

callbacks.how: Three lamps are enough because the eye keeps only three signals.

stations.goal: The eye turns any light into three signals. Lights with the same three signals look the same.
stations.object: A spectrum with the three cone curves, a pure light A and a lamp B made of red plus green.
stations.action: Adjusts the red and green parts of lamp B until its three cone signals equal those of light A.
stations.surprise: Two physically different lights give identical signals and identical colour.
controls: Red and green amounts of lamp B (one pair of sliders)
tries: Match light A using only the red and green lamps.
Move light A to another wavelength and match it again.
stations.takeaway: Pure yellow light and a red-plus-green mix are physically different but look identical, and lights of this kind are called metamers. This is why three lamps are enough for a screen.
stations.source: Cone curves are simplified bell shapes. Both swatches are computed from the three signals with the same rule, so they are approximate but comparable.

page.title: Three kinds of cone
page.text: The retina has three kinds of colour receptor. Each answers to a broad range of wavelengths, most strongly to long, medium or short ones. A light, however complex, leaves the eye as three signals.

page.title: Different lights, same signals
page.text: Pure yellow light excites the long and medium cones together, and so does a mix of red and green light in the right proportion. The brain then receives the same three signals from both lights and cannot tell them apart.

questions.q: How many signals does the eye keep for any light?
questions.why: Three kinds of cone, three signals. Everything else about the light is lost.
traps: One signal would be enough for brightness alone; three kinds of cone each send their own.
The rainbow is often drawn with seven colours, but the eye keeps only three signals for any light.
If the eye recorded every wavelength, different lights could never look identical; it keeps only three numbers.

questions.q: Two lights with different spectra look identical when...
options: they give the same three cone signals
questions.why: The eye keeps only the three signals. Same signals, same colour.
traps: Equal brightness is not enough: two lights can be equally bright and still look like different colours.
Two different pure wavelengths look different colours; what decides a match is the three cone signals.

questions.q: Why can a screen with three lamps show yellow without any yellow light?
options: Red plus green gives the same cone signals as yellow light
The screen has a hidden yellow lamp
Yellow is not a real colour
questions.why: The eye only keeps three signals. Same signals, same colour, whatever the light was made of.
traps: It seems that yellow should need yellow light; but the eye only keeps three signals, and red plus green gives the same ones.
A hidden yellow lamp would explain it, but a screen has only red, green and blue; red plus green does the job.
Yellow is as real a colour as any other; on a screen it is made from red and green, but it still looks yellow.

questions.q: Two lights with different spectra that look identical are called...
questions.why: Metamerism is what makes screens and printing possible.
traps: Complementary colours are real, but they are pairs that sit opposite each other, not lights that look the same.
Primaries are the few colours you mix others from, not two lights that look identical.
Saturated means vivid, far from grey; it says nothing about two different lights looking the same.

questions.q: A yellow sign and a yellow screen beside it look exactly the same colour to you. What can you be sure of?
options: They give your cones the same three signals
They send out exactly the same light
They both send out a single yellow wavelength
They are equally bright, nothing more
questions.why: Looking identical means the same three cone signals. The light itself can differ: the screen makes its yellow from red and green.
traps: Identical-looking lights seem to be identical light, but different mixtures can give the same three signals.
A pure yellow wavelength would look yellow, but the screen makes yellow from red and green light and still matches.
Equal brightness alone does not make two colours look the same; all three cone signals must match.

questions.q: Why can a screen show the yellow of a sunflower with only red, green and blue lamps?
options: Because the sunflower reflects only red and green light
Because the screen has a tiny yellow filter
Because red plus green gives the eye the same three signals as the flower's yellow
Because the camera that took the photo saw only yellow
questions.why: The eye keeps three signals. A screen does not copy the light of the flower: it makes a light that gives the same three signals.
traps: It sounds tidy if the flower sent out the screen's two lights, but the screen does not need to copy the light: only the three signals.
A hidden yellow part would explain it, but a screen has only red, green and blue: the match happens in the eye.
What a camera saw does not decide it; the screen works because the eye keeps only three signals.

relations.note: An ink is defined by which of the three lights it removes.
Lights start from dark and add; inks start from white and take away.
Hue, saturation and lightness re-describe the three lamp numbers.
Judging lightness and hue by eye is where context misleads.
The numbers stay fixed; the appearance does not.
The matching experiment uses added lights.
Three cone signals are the reason three lamps are enough.
Young’s three receptors of 1802, made operable.
Munsell’s ordering is the ancestor of the three dials.
